[b][u]Announcement From the Ministry of Defence[/u][/b]

The Ministry of Defence announces that its tank and drone development programmes have concluded and delivered promising results.

The tank programme has developed the T-90 tank, Dhornaper's first third-generation main battle tank. Built on the existing T-72, thr T-90 is heavily modernised with better armor, a more powerful engine, and a much better fire control system. The tank will enter serial production soon and will begin to make its way into the military, replacing the T-72 in some units.

The drone programme has delivered multiple promising drones and innovated on the armed forces' doctrine.

The first drone developed is the "Orlan-10", a reconnaissance drone. It is designed to detect cellular and radio communications and integrates with the existing RB-341V to perform this role and extend the range of their RB-341V jammer. It also can provide information through its onboard cameras and sensors. It's designed for short ranges and tactical use and as such has a range of 120km, maximum altitude of 1.5km, and a maximum speed of 150km/h.

The second drone developed is the Lancet. It is primarily a loitering munition but is also capable of reconnaissance. As a loitering munition, it is capable of flying for long periods, independently capable of identifying a target, and striking it with a maximum payload of 5kg. As a reconaissance drone, it can identify its location from satellite navigation or its onboard sensors and camera and provide information to ground controllers with its camera and sensors. It is designed for tactical use and has a range of 40km, a maximum altitude of 2.5km, and a speed of 110km/h in cruise and 300km/h in dive.

The last drone developed is the Geran-2, which is solely a loitering munition. It has a maximum payload of 90kg, a range of 1,000km, maximum altitude of 4km, and speed of 185km/h. It can be both remotely controlled to loiter in a specific area or use inertial navigation to reach its target. It is designed for strategic targets and attacks against enemy infrastructure in rear areas.

The development of the drones, after following events in recent wars, has modified the armed forces doctrine in important ways. Drones are not expected to replace aircraft or artillery. Drones are expected to complement artillery by providing targetting information and by giving smaller units a quick way to operate a substitute for artillery as circumstances require it. Drones are expected to substitute air strikes in enemy air space where air defences make sorties too dangerous. Separately, drones will chiefly be used to saturate air defences.

These innovations are expected to improve the capability of the armed forces but, contrary to proclamations from other nations, the armed forces does not expect developments in drone warfare to radically alter the existing method of war.
